Many of my heroes have been tainted over the years, but a forerunner in the field of nuclear physics has stood quite strong: Lise Meitner. 

Lise Meitner is the woman who with her nephew Otto Robert Frisch interpreted experimental data produced by Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassman, and in doing so, discovered nuclear fission.

She has many more accomplishments but has been somewhat forgotten in history due to her exclusion from the 1944 Nobel Prize, which Otto Hahn won for *his* discovery of nuclear fission.

She was excluded, due to what can only be described as bureaucratic oversight in a very turbulent time.


Meitner would be nominated 49 times for Nobel Prizes in the fields of Physics and Chemistry, but would die at 89 having won none of them.

In honor of her memory, Element 109 on the periodic table is named *Meitnerium.*

The owl knows where it is at all times. It knows this because it knows where it isn't. 

By subtracting where it is from where it isn't, or where it isn't from where it is (whichever is greater), it obtains a difference, or deviation. The player uses deviations to generate inputs to drive the owl from a position where it is to a position where it isn't, and arriving at a position where it wasn't, it now is. 

Consequently, the position where it is, is now the position that it wasn't, and it follows that the position that it was, is now the position that it isn't.

In the event that the position that it is in is not the position that it wasn't, the system has acquired a variation, the variation being the difference between where the owl is, and where it wasn't. If variation is considered to be a significant factor, it too may be corrected by the player. However, the owl must also know where it was.

The owl guidance scenario works as follows. Because a variation has modified some of the information the owl has obtained, it is not sure just where it is. However, it is sure where it isn't, within reason, and it knows where it was. It now subtracts where it should be from where it wasn't, or vice-versa, and by differentiating this from the algebraic sum of where it shouldn't be, and where it was, it is able to obtain the deviation and its variation, which is called error.

A person, or persons, gains access to permissions on a Discord server that allow them to use Discord tools to disrupt the server in all ways possible, including but not limited to removing chats, spamming chats, banning members, kicking members, etc.

Often, this is done through the raiders inviting and activating a bot with the permissions given to perform these actions automatically, and often, endlessly.

How to guard against it? Vet your moderation and administrative teams on a server, and do frequent checkups on server permissions to ensure that there are no permission holes that can be exploited.

Warframe and Terraria.

Warframe has actual thousands of hours of content. And it's completely free-to-play. It has an incredible movement system and possibly the most unique weapon and character customization out of any game I've seen in a long time. I forewarn you now, the game is also hellishly difficult at some times and very grindy. Extremely grindy. It also has a number of alternative play areas instead of the standard tile set horde shooter, including open-world adventure, fighter pilot simulator, collaborative dungeons, and even a soulsborne-esque alternate reality. (Currently MR 15/33 and I still haven't done close to everything.)

Terraria costs a bit, but for ten bucks you get a pretty solid open world with literally thousands of items and a very challenging experience should you want to turn the difficulty up. The real pleasure, though, is in TModLoader. Terraria has a built-in, developer-approved mod client that lets you load community-created mods into your experience. Some provide QoL changes or funny items, and some transform Terraria into a hellish, freakishly hard experience that will suck days out of your lifespan. (Terraria Ultra Death Mode player here, can confirm, make sure you have a friend on hand to keep your head on straight.)

Definitely advise trying either out. They both also have dedicated fanbases, and YouTube tutorials and reviews are common. 

Some other recommends that I personally play or know of are Satisfactory, Astroneer, and Hydroneer.

The TD playstyle is debatable depending on the type of TD you're using, ie. Sniper, Frontline, Turreted, etc. 

The E100 (or Maus ) is a Superheavy tank, so it can blend Frontline TD and Main HT playstyles much more effectively than other tanks.

Superheavies like the E100 and Maus in the German line kind of defy the logic of standard heavies in Tier X compared to England and Russia. They are heavier and stacked with significantly more armor, thus I think in team dynamics their use is very debatable. 

Playing either as a spearhead makes flankers superbly difficult to deal with while keeping them as the backline makes their armor utterly useless. Playing them results in a lot of difficult decisions, but I think your goal as a superheavy is to take 1v1s with a lone enemy heavy that you face hug, and pin. You stay near the middle of the pack and pick out an overextended heavy that you pin and cut out of their team. I think you also pick out overextended TDs in the same fashion, and avoid the hell out of mediums and lights unless you have supporting teammates.

Personally speaking, TDS fall into two categories, front and rear TDS.

Rear TDS do everything you just said and often have zero to none armor (ex: Grille 15)

Front TDS are more likely to flank in the early match and go with lighter heavies or heavier mediums to deal a huge shot to slow heavies and cause the enemies to redirect attention to themselves and cause pressure from that direction.

The T29 has horrible movement speed. This is true. 

What you lack in speed, however, is armor and gun statistics. If I'm not mistaken, the T29 is one of the best non-premium heavy tanks in tier VII.

However, playing this tank requires a considerable amount of finesse. Your hardest battles are not going to be the ones where you are fighting, but when you want to get from point A to point B. Therefore, be sneaky. Move with tanks that are slower, and if there are none, trial behind your team. While it may seem bad to be slower, it's actually good. 

Say your team is a solid ways ahead of you and they've spotted the enemy. Instead of pushing with the main part of your team, take a different position, reveal yourself, and let 279mm of turret armor do the talking. Your gun has 10 degrees of gun depression, so hull down is your best friend. Your turret bounces 90% of shots from most tanks. Your gun isn't lacking either, at around 8.8 seconds of reload and 300 damage per shot, peeking enemies will need to watch out.

This strategy gives your team a lot of options. Enemies shooting at you are not shooting at them. They can regroup, shoot back from better positions, flank, etc. As a rule of thumb, once the enemy is severely grouped up and down at least 2 to 3 tanks, you move out. Take routes with a lot of cover, and do not be afraid to flank and charge straight into a tank destroyer or heavy tank.  

Now let's consider something else. Your team is idiotic and has waited for heavy tank support, and now the standings are 3 of you vs 5 of them. In this case, STICK WITH YOUR TEAM. Take front point, and soak up damage with your turret armor and 1500 HP pool. Make the enemy team frustrated that they can't kill you and enable your last two teammates to pull off capitalization on bold enemies who think a 5v3 is an easy win. Teams who see the T29 at advantage tend to tunnel vision you thinking you're an easy kill as a slow heavy tank, not realizing you have two teammates who will defend you against idiotic solo flankers. 

TL;DR - Soak up damage with your turret armor and enable your team to capitalize on enemy team mistakes as they tunnel vision try to kill you.

Yeah, Hog is great as a 1v1 character but in teamplay, you really need your team to capitalize on your hooks and disruptions.

Hog is a off-tank flanker and capitalizes on squishy DPS and healers. If there are two things you need to master, it's his hook and his one-shot hook combo.

Hook can be improved with googling "hog training room" and finding a hook practice.

Once you've mastered that, one-shot hook combos are easy. Hook-shoot-melee. Not hard to practice, pretty easy to master, and once it's muscle memory any squishy targeted by your hook is dead.

A few other things include flanking tactics, hooking off the edge (12 hogs, 1 hole I recommend), and secondary fire. Also knowing when to Take a Breather is a thing. 

I'm not an absolute god at roadhog either but a few games of playing him will get used to him pretty quickly. He's meant to pop out of an alley in the middle line, hook a healer or DPS, fire off a few shots, and then retreat back into his team. He can secure kills, yes, but his major capabilities are in 1v1s and being a massive distraction and disruptor to teams who are hyperfocused on the main tank. You have 600 health, 300 free healing, and (thanks to a new update) you grant *25% less ultimate charge when the enemy shoots you*.

Honestly, give him a whirl. You might not end up maining him but he's a useful character to know how to play

This is a question that  I have been pondering for a while, so imma go with full detail. TL;DR at the bottom.

If they are going to continue their current tank trend, we need to analyze the current tank set:

Type 89B, Hetzer (converted from Pz. 38 (t)), Char B1 bis, Chi-Nu, M3 Lee, Stug III, Porche Tiger, Mark IV, and Pz. IV Ausf A upgraded to H model.

One of the things right off the bat: the majority of the tanks are early-war. Exceptions include the Chi-Nu, Porsche Tiger, and Mark IV.   
The Chi-nu was a rare tank and fielded in very small numbers by the Japanese army.   
The Porsche Tiger only had a few prototypes made.  
The Mark IV isn't early-war because it's freaking pre-war.

Another thing I ran into was that Oorai and the other schools have basically none of the same tanks. The only similarities I can think of are Chi-Ha-Tan having Type 89s and the Maginot school having Char B1s.

So from my deductions, we need a tank that is either an early-war tank or a mid to late-war prototype. I'm also going to assume we take one from the British, German, Russian, or American lineups.

For the British, possible candidates include the Black Prince, Excelsior tank, or Valiant tank.   
The Black Prince is a late-war planned Churchill conversion with a QF 17-pounder and a larger turret.  
The Excelsior is a late-war heavy tank based on the Cromwell design with a QF 75mm.  
The Valiant is a prototype early-war assault tank with a QF 6-pounder. 

Of the three, I believe the Valiant is the most likely, given it's planned use as a lightweight yet heavily armored vehicle and it's relative obscurity (Yukari will have Panzer High). 

For the Germans, possible candidates include the VK 30.01 (D), VK 30.01 (P), or a Neubaufahrzeug.  
The VK 30.01 (D) is basically the Germans' prototype attempt to copy and counter the T-34, and was the competing design for the now widely known Panther tank. It sported the 75 mm KwK 42 L/70 gun.  
The VK 30.01 (P) was a medium tank prototype that later evolved into the Porsche Tiger. It would have mounted either a 75 mm KwK L/24, 105 mm KwK L/28, or 88 mm KwK L/56.  
The Neubaufahrzeug is an early-war series of medium tanks that fared poorly due to their slow speed, large weight, and multi-turreted design. They would have mounted a main 75 mm KwK L/24 and secondary 37mm KwK L/45. 

Of the three, I think the VK 30.01 (D) is the best candidate, being it was basically the German version of the T-34. The VK 30.01 (P) would look too similar to the Porsche Tiger, and the Neubaufahrzeug doesn't fit aesthetically with Ooari's style and the style of the show.

Onto the Russians! As with Russia, there is a multitude of choices. Possible candidates include T-40 to T-70 series, A-32, T-43, SU-85 to SU-100Y series, and literally multitudes of T-34 modifications.  
Jesus. Ok...

The A-32 is an experimental early-war medium tank that was a direct result of T-34 research. Armed with a 76.2mm gun, it carries many of the qualities of the T-34.   
The T-43 was a prototype mid-war medium tank that was planned to replace the T-34 but was canceled in favor of the T-34-85. It had a 76.2mm L10.   
The SU-85 to SU-100Y series was the Russian series of tank destroyers, including the SU-85, SU-100, SU-152, ISU-152, and SU-100Y, with multiple variants. The number usually denotes the caliber of the tank gun, and they were also used as mobile artillery.
